name: Light Brownish Vinaceous
lede: Light Brownish Vinaceous is a pale, dusty pink from Ridgway's 1912 atlas, sitting closer to Silver Pink than to any true brown.

sections.title: A dusty pink, not a brown
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 atlas carries this tone on plate XXXIX, hue 5‴ [1]. The 1955 ISCC-NBS dictionary groups it under block 8, naming it grayish pink, 2.5 units from Ridgway's reading, its Munsell notation given as 7.1R 7.4/2.7 [1].

Despite the word "brownish" in its name, its nearest neighbor in our library is [[silver-pink]], about 3.2 units away and redder, followed by [[pale-purplish-vinaceous]], almost the same color at 3.6 units [2]. [[pale-blush]] and [[light-vinaceous-fawn]] sit a little further, each about 4.2 units off and more yellow [2]. *Vinaceous*, wine-colored, is the operative word; the brown reads as a dusty cast over pink, not a separate hue [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds a matching color in 117 of 23,781 paintings, about 0.49 percent, as photographed, more common than 56 percent of the named colors tracked [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, present in 1.2 percent of the 1,674 paintings from that decade, 2.8 times its museums' expected rate [3].

Inside a painting it most often hides, in 45 percent of its 82 clearly-ranked appearances, a rank computed within each canvas so varnish cannot fake it [3]. It is also most over-represented in Indian paintings, 2.7 times the expected rate, found in 12 of the archive's 721 [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and the match is a computed color reading, not a pigment identification [3].
